claims.text: A Ti-containing coating can be prepared on Q235 steel by laser cladding.
Ti additions in a laser-cladded coating refine the near-surface microstructure of Q235 steel.
Ti additions minimize micro-cracking in the laser-cladded layer.
Smaller grains and fewer micro-cracks facilitate formation of a dense, continuous, and adherent passivating oxide film.
Cracks and similar defects act as initiation sites for corrosion.
Ti promotes formation of stable Ti-rich oxides in the corrosion-product layer.
Ti-rich oxides integrate with iron oxides and improve the continuity and protectiveness of the corrosion-product layer.
The combined reduction in defect sites and formation of Ti-rich oxides decreases corrosion relative to untreated Q235 steel.
The effect of Ti content in laser-cladded coatings on Q235 steel microstructure and corrosion resistance has been studied in 3.5 wt.% NaCl.
The Ti-enhanced laser-cladded specimens will have lower corrosion-related mass loss than untreated Q235 steel.
The Ti-enhanced laser-cladded specimens will exhibit improved electrochemical impedance relative to untreated Q235 steel.
The treated specimens will retain a more homogeneous and crack-free microstructure at room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures.
The proposed corrosion suppression applies in neutral chloride-containing solutions.
The coating's passivation mechanism remains effective at temperatures up to approximately 100 °C.
Temperatures or corrosive environments beyond the coating's operational limits may defeat the passivation mechanism.

Comparing treated specimens only with untreated Q235 under identical exposures tests the combined coating treatment but does not separately isolate the causal contribution of Ti from laser cladding and the rest of the coating.
